content.title: About
content.content: Collards (leafy cabbage) are dark‑green leafy vegetables from the Brassicaceae family. The frozen product is quickly blanched and then sautéed in vegetable oil, preserving its bright color, crisp texture, and a mildly bitter flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Collards are often called a “super‑green” because of their high vitamin and mineral content.
Unlike spinach, collard leaves stay crunchy even after cooking.
Traditionally grown in warm climates, freezing allows year‑round availability.
Cooking in oil enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins A, K and E.
Collard leaves can grow up to 60 cm long, but frozen products usually use smaller chopped pieces.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: High in vitamin A
items.content: Vitamin A supports vision, immune function, and skin health.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Capsaicin and carotenoids protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Minerals: calcium and iron
items.content: Calcium strengthens bones, while iron is vital for oxygen transport.

items.title: Allergy to vegetable oils
items.content: The product may contain traces of canola, sunflower or olive oil, which can trigger reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Elevated sodium content
items.content: Salt added during sautéing can raise sodium levels; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Collards contain oxalates, which may contribute to kidney stone formation in predisposed persons.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the frozen collards in a skillet, microwave, or steamer. They work well added to soups, stews, pasta, omelets, or as a side dish for meat and fish. A squeeze of lemon juice or a sprinkle of fresh herbs brightens the flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. After thawing, use within 1–2 days and do not refreeze. Discard if you notice off‑odors or discoloration.

macaroni-or-pasta-salad-with-egg.title: Macaroni or Pasta Salad with Egg

content.title: About
content.content: Macaroni or pasta salad with egg is a cold dish where cooked pasta (or macaroni) is mixed with hard‑boiled eggs, mayonnaise or yogurt, fresh vegetables and seasonings. It is popular as a light lunch, snack or picnic food.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Short‑shaped pasta such as rotini, penne or farfalle is commonly used because it holds the dressing well.
Eggs add not only flavor but also a complete set of proteins and vitamins.
Different countries use different dressings: in Russia – mayonnaise, in Italy – olive oil with lemon, in the US – a yogurt‑based sauce.
The salad can be prepared ahead of time and keeps well in the fridge for 2‑3 days.
Fresh herbs like parsley, dill or basil boost aroma and make the dish more vibrant.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Eggs and pasta provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Carbohydrates from pasta give a quick source of energy, making the salad a good pre‑exercise option.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs contain vitamin B12, while whole‑grain pasta supplies B1, B2, B3, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish provides iron, phosphorus and selenium from eggs and magnesium from pasta, supporting nervous system function.

items.title: Digestive benefits
items.content: Adding fresh vegetables (cucumber, tomato, green onion) increases fiber, promoting healthy digestion.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to eggs, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Eggs are high in cholesterol; people with elevated cholesterol levels should limit their intake.

items.title: Food poisoning risk
items.content: Improperly cooked or stored eggs can harbor salmonella; use fresh eggs and keep the salad refrigerated.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Traditional pasta contains gluten, so those with celiac disease should use gluten‑free alternatives (rice or corn pasta).

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled, often in individual bowls or cups. It can be eaten on its own, with bread or crackers, or as a side dish to meat or fish.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C. It remains tasty for up to 3 days. Stir before serving to redistribute the dressing.

content.title: About
content.content: Pork belly is the cut from the underside of a pig, consisting of layers of meat, fat, and skin. It is prized for its tenderness, juiciness, and rich flavor, and is used in Asian, American, and European cuisines.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pork belly is one of the fattiest cuts of meat, making it ideal for slow cooking and achieving a crispy crackling.
In China, braised pork belly (红烧肉) is considered a national delicacy.
In the United States pork belly is the base for bacon, which is cured, smoked, and sliced.
Korean cuisine features samgyeopsal – thick slices of pork belly grilled at the table.
The fat in pork belly contains both monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that enhance flavor when cooked properly.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Pork belly provides high‑quality animal protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains thiamine (B1), riboflavin (B2), pyridoxine (B6) and cobalamin (B12), which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals are important for immune health, DNA synthesis, and oxygen transport.

items.title: Polyunsaturated fatty acids
items.content: When consumed in moderation, the fat can promote satiety and improve the taste profile of dishes.

items.title: Collagen
items.content: The skin and connective tissue contain collagen, which may benefit joint and skin health when cooked slowly.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Pork belly is rich in saturated fat; excessive intake can raise cholesterol levels and increase cardiovascular risk.

items.title: Calorie dense
items.content: Because of its fat, it is very calorie‑dense, so portion control is recommended.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked pork may harbor pathogens such as Salmonella. Cook to an internal temperature of at least 71 °C.

items.title: Pig meat allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to pork proteins.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pork belly can be roasted, braised, fried, smoked, or steamed. Popular methods include slow‑roasting for crispy crackling, marinating and frying as bacon, or cooking in teriyaki or sweet‑sour sauces. It is cut into cubes, strips, or large slabs depending on the recipe.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh pork belly in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C, wrapped in plastic or in an airtight container, for up to 3‑5 days. For longer storage, freeze in a sealed bag at –18 °C for up to 6 months. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration before cooking.

rice-brown-with-carrots-and-tomatoes-and.title: Brown Rice with Carrots and Tomatoes (no added fat)

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice is a whole‑grain product obtained by removing only the outer hull of the grain. In this dish the rice is cooked together with carrots and tomatoes or a tomato‑based sauce without any added fat, making it low‑calorie and nutrient‑dense.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice retains the bran and germ, providing more fiber, vitamins, and minerals than white rice.
Carrots are rich in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
Tomatoes are a good source of lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that helps protect cells.
Cooking without added fat preserves the natural flavors of the ingredients and reduces calorie content.
Brown rice has a lower glycemic index than white rice, helping to maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate cholesterol levels.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Complex carbohydrates provide sustained energy, which is important for active individuals.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Carrots and tomatoes add vitamin A, vitamin C, potassium, and magnesium, supporting immunity and muscle function.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: The absence of added fat makes the dish suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Lycopene from tomatoes and beta‑carotene from carrots protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Rice allergy
items.content: A small number of people may be allergic to rice, experiencing skin rashes or gastrointestinal symptoms.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Brown rice contains phytic acid, which can reduce the absorption of certain minerals when consumed in excess.

items.title: Food interactions
items.content: Tomatoes can enhance the effect of some medications, such as anticoagulants; consult a healthcare professional if you take medicines.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish as a side to meat, fish, or legumes, or use it as a base for vegetarian bowls. It reheats well in the microwave or on the stovetop, and fresh herbs can be added for extra aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. When frozen, it can be stored for up to 2 months after cooling to room temperature.

content.title: About
content.content: Light spinach dip is a smooth sauce made from fresh spinach, low‑fat cottage cheese and gentle spices. It has a mild, slightly tangy flavor and creamy texture, perfect for diet‑friendly meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Spinach is rich in iron, vitamin K and folate, making it a staple of healthy eating.
Light dips often replace cream with cottage cheese or yogurt, reducing calories.
Spinach dip is commonly used in Mediterranean cuisine as a sauce for vegetables and seafood.
The sodium content in light versions is usually lower than in traditional mayonnaise‑based sauces.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Spinach provides lutein and zeaxanthin, which support eye health.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamin C and vitamin A in spinach help strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Low‑calorie protein source
items.content: Cottage cheese adds animal protein without excess fat.

items.title: Digestive aid
items.content: Fiber from spinach promotes healthy bowel function.

items.title: Cholesterol reduction
items.content: Low saturated fat content helps maintain healthy cholesterol levels.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cottage cheese may trigger reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Spinach contains oxalates, which in large amounts can contribute to kidney stone formation.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some ready‑made versions add salt; those monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dip with fresh vegetables, whole‑grain crackers, or use it as a sauce for fish and chicken. It also works well in sandwiches or as a salad dressing.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the dip in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: White beans in cans are a ready‑to‑eat product made from selected bean varieties that are pre‑cooked and sealed in their own juice with added vegetable fat. The beans have a mild, slightly nutty flavor and a soft, creamy texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Canned white beans retain most of their nutrients thanks to rapid heat processing.
The added fat enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins and gives a richer taste.
Beans belong to the legume family, one of the oldest cultivated crops worldwide.
In different regions white beans are known as "cannellini," "navy beans," or simply "white peas."
Canned beans are shelf‑stable, requiring no refrigeration and offering a long shelf life.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: A 100 g serving provides about 7 g of protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: These minerals are essential for hemoglobin formation and nerve function.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Beans raise blood sugar slowly, which is beneficial for people with pre‑diabetes.

items.title: Added fat improves absorption of vitamins A, D, E, and K
items.content: The vegetable fat in the can helps the body utilize fat‑soluble vitamins more efficiently.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Canned products often contain added salt; choose low‑sodium versions if you monitor sodium intake.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Those on low‑fat diets should account for the added fat in the calorie count.

items.title: Bacterial contamination from damaged cans
items.content: Bulging or leaking cans can harbor botulism; discard any compromised containers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Beans can be eaten straight from the can, added to salads, soups, stews, or used as a filling for wraps. It is advisable to drain the liquid and, if desired, rinse the beans with cold water before use.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the unopened can in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, transfer beans to an airtight container and refrigerate for up to 3–4 days.
